TITLE: Lower Bounds for Unconstrained Regression Formulations
PROPOSAL: We prove a lower bound on the sample complexity of Constrained Weighted Least-Squares estimation in the setting of realizable regression. Specifically, we assume that the ground-truth Shapley values lie in a known convex set and the regression matrix $\bm{Z}$ is nearly incoherent, and we show that the sample size needs to be at least $\Omega(d\log(d))$ to consistently estimate the Constrained Weighted Least-Squares solution. To obtain this bound, we use the Le Cam's lemma and a new extension of the Fano's inequality to the constrained setting. Our result provides the first non-asymptotic bound for this fundamental problem and implies that sampling strategies with fewer than $O(d\log(d))$ samples are not sufficient to achieve consistency.
CONTROLS: We compare our result with the upper bound of LeverageSHAP. We also experiment with randomly permutations of the rows of the regression matrix and compare the attained sample complexity.
COST: 168
PREDICTION: We expect to establish the proved lower bound on the sample complexity, while the upper bound from LeverageSHAP will hold for slightly more than $O(d\log(d))$ samples. The randomized permutation experiments will likely reveal that standard kernel weights, used in LeverageSHAP, are more efficient than uniform weights.

TITLE: Empirical Study of Sampling Distributions for KernelSHAP
PROPOSAL: We carry out an extensive empirical study of the effect of different sampling distributions on the accuracy and computational efficiency of KernelSHAP. We implement and compare several weighted, unweighted, and adaptive sampling strategies on various real-world datasets, including the adult, credit-guess, and compas datasets from the COMPAS project. Our experiments examine the benefits and drawbacks of paired sampling, unconditional sampling and sampling without replacement, and we provide insights into which sampling strategy performs best for different baseline models and data domains.
CONTROLS: We use the default implementation of KernelSHAP with the above-mentioned sampling strategies. We also compare our results with the fixed design estimator for Constrained Weighted Least-Squares regression.
COST: 1890
PREDICTION: We anticipate that paired sampling will outperform unconditional sampling in terms of accuracy and efficiency, while adaptive sampling will yield high accuracy but require significant computational resources. The results will further suggest that, in some cases, the additional overhead of paired sampling justifies its benefits.

TITLE: Bounding the Estimation Error of Unbiased KernelSHAP
PROPOSAL: We derive a non-asymptotic bias-variance bound for the Unbiased KernelSHAP estimator, which includes a novel concentration inequality for the estimated Shapley values. Our analysis assumes that the kernel weights are of bounded range and uses the Martingale Central Limit Theorem to establish the variance bound. We then use the Le Cam's lemma to relate the bias and variance bounds to the L2-risk of the estimator.
CONTROLS: We compare our result with the known bound for the original KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP, highlighting the effect of bias correction on estimation accuracy.
COST: 2332.8
PREDICTION: We expect to show that the bias correction in Unbiased KernelSHAP comes at a significant cost in terms of variance, but our derived bound will also reveal the benefits of the bias correction in reducing the L2-risk.

PROPOSAL: We revisit the derivation of the bias-variance bound for Unbiased KernelSHAP and identify a more efficient method to establish the variance part of the bound using the Gaussian concentration inequality. This allows us to tighten the bias-variance tradeoff and obtain a more favorable bound, which should help to better understand the estimation error of Unbiased KernelSHAP.
CONTROLS: We compare our revised bound with the original bound and the bound for the original KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP.

TITLE: Analyzing High-Dimensional Shapley Values with Leverage-score Sampling
PROPOSAL: We investigate the potential of Leverage-score sampling for estimating high-dimensional Shapley values with LeverageSHAP. We demonstrate how to adapt Leverage-score sampling to the Shapley value setting and provide theoretical guarantees for the accuracy of the estimation. Our analysis assumes that the kernel weights are of bounded range and uses the Martingale Central Limit Theorem to establish the variance bound. We then perform experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets to evaluate the performance of LeverageSHAP with Leverage-score sampling.
CONTROLS: We compare our results with the standard KernelSHAP and other sampling strategies.
COST: 3130
PREDICTION: We expect LeverageSHAP with Leverage-score sampling to outperform standard KernelSHAP in high-dimensional settings due to its improved efficiency and accuracy, but may require significant computational resources.

TITLE: Fast and Accurate Estimation of Shapley Values with Gradient Boosting
PROPOSAL: We propose a new algorithm that uses gradient boosting to estimate Shapley values efficiently and accurately. The algorithm uses a set of weak models to approximate the feature contributions and then combines them to obtain the final Shapley values. We provide theoretical guarantees for the accuracy of the estimation and demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments on various real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: We compare our results with standard KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP, as well as other models and algorithms.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: We expect our algorithm to outperform standard KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP in terms of speed and accuracy, especially in high-dimensional settings.

TITLE: Understanding Shapley Values in Deep Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: We investigate the properties of Shapley values in deep neural networks and provide insights into their behavior. We analyze the relationship between Shapley values and saliency maps, and demonstrate that Shapley values can be used to identify important features and patterns in the data. Our results provide a deeper understanding of Shapley values and their applications in deep learning.
CONTROLS: We compare our results with other explanation methods, such as saliency maps and feature importance.
